stem:
Chipo grows 200 tomato plants near Masvingo. She records three problems each week. Bored fruits contain caterpillars; wilted plants collapse suddenly while still green; the leaf spots are dark brown with rings.

| Week | Plants with bored fruit | Plants wilted | Plants with ringed leaf spots |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 2 | 0 | 3 |
| 2 | 5 | 4 | 9 |
| 3 | 11 | 9 | 18 |
| 4 | 16 | 15 | 30 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Name the fungal disease that causes dark brown leaf spots with rings on tomatoes.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage of plants wilted in week 4.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: A wilted stem placed in a glass of water releases milky threads. Which group of organism causes the wilt?

options.rationale: Fungal wilts do not stream ooze like this.
Viruses cause mosaics and curling, not ooze.
Root-knot nematodes cause galls, not ooze.

parts.explanation: Streaming bacterial ooze shows bacterial wilt.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Name the moth whose larvae bore into tomato fruits.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Describe the life cycle of the pest named in (d).

points.description: Eggs laid singly on young leaves, buds and flowers.
Larvae feed on buds and flowers and bore into the fruit.
Larvae pupate in the soil; moths emerge and lay eggs (complete metamorphosis).

parts.explanation: Egg, larva, pupa in soil, adult.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Explain why spraying a fungicide will not control the wilt.

points.description: The wilt is caused by bacteria, which fungicides do not kill.
The bacteria are inside the water-conducting tissue / in the soil, where sprays cannot reach (there is no chemical cure).

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: State **two** precautions Chipo must observe when spraying tomatoes that are close to harvest.

points.description: Observe the pre-harvest interval on the label before picking.
Wear protective clothing / spray in calm weather / keep people out of the field until the re-entry time / wash fruit.

parts.label: (h)
parts.stem: Describe an integrated programme Chipo could follow from before planting to harvest to control the pests and diseases of her tomatoes.

points.description: Before planting: rotate away from tomato-family crops (and land with bacterial wilt) for several seasons; choose resistant varieties and clean, healthy seedlings.
Prepare well-drained land; remove weed hosts such as nightshades and old crop residues.
Space and stake plants for air movement; water at the base (drip or furrow) so leaves stay dry, reducing early blight.
Scout regularly (twice a week), recording bored fruit, wilted plants and leaf spots, and compare with action levels.
Remove and destroy wilted plants with their soil and pick off spotted lower leaves; disinfect tools and wash hands.
Use a protectant fungicide against early blight when weather favours it, renewing after rain.
Against bollworm: destroy damaged fruit, use pheromone traps to time action, encourage natural enemies, and spray a suitable insecticide on young larvae only when scouting shows it is needed.
Observe pre-harvest intervals, wear protective clothing, and after harvest destroy residues and rotate.

Some relevant points explained, partly developed or only partly applied to the situation; any judgement is simple or one-sided.
Simple statements or a list of points with little explanation or application.

parts.explanation: Prevention, monitoring, cultural, biological and chemical methods in order, with reasons.

explanation: Interpret field records of tomato pests and diseases, describe a pest life cycle and plan integrated control.
hints: Which group of organism makes ringed spots, and which causes sudden wilt?
For the long part, organise your answer from before planting to harvest.

stem: Tendai grows 3.5 ha of maize on sandy soil near Gokwe. Short plants with red flowers appear among the maize each February, and a corner of the field is full of couch grass. He compares weeding by hand twice (20 person-days per hectare each time) with a programme of a pre-emergence herbicide at 1.8 L/ha plus 1 person-day of spraying and one hand weeding of 8 person-days per hectare. Assume labour costs US\$4.50 per person-day and the herbicide US\$9 per litre.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Name the parasitic weed with red flowers.

parts.label: (b)

options.rationale: Couch grass is a grass and perennial.
Sedges have triangular stems, like nut grass.
Correct: it spreads by rhizomes and stolons.

parts.explanation: Couch grass is a perennial grass.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the volume of herbicide needed for the whole field, in litres.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the cost per hectare of the herbicide programme, to the nearest cent.
parts.explanation: Herbicide 1.8 × 9 = US\$16.20; spraying 1 × 4.50 = US\$4.50; hand weeding 8 × 4.50 = US\$36; total US\$56.70.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Herbicide 1.8 × 9 = US\$16.20; spraying 1 × 4.50 = US\$4.50; hand weeding 8 × 4.50 = US\$36; total US\$56.70.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Calculate how much Tendai saves on the whole field by using the herbicide programme instead of hand weeding twice. Give your answer to the nearest cent.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Explain why a pre-emergence herbicide should be applied to moist soil soon after planting.

points.description: It forms a layer in the surface soil that kills weed seedlings as they germinate, which needs moisture to work.
Applied before crop and weeds emerge, it keeps the crop weed-free in its critical early weeks.

parts.explanation: Moist soil activates the layer; early control.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Explain why couch grass is not killed by hoeing or by a contact herbicide.

points.description: It regrows from its rhizomes and stolons, which hoeing cuts up and spreads.
A contact herbicide kills only the leaves it touches and does not reach the rhizomes (a systemic herbicide is needed).

parts.label: (h)
parts.stem: Discuss how Tendai could reduce witchweed and couch grass in this field over the next few seasons.

points.description: Witchweed seeds stay alive in the soil for many years, so control must continue over several seasons.
Rotate maize with trap crops such as groundnuts, cowpeas, soya beans or cotton, which cause suicidal germination of witchweed seeds.
Hand-pull witchweed before it flowers and sets seed, and destroy it, so the seed store shrinks.
Improve soil fertility with manure or compost and nitrogen fertiliser, which reduces witchweed attack; use tolerant varieties and clean seed.
Treat couch grass with a systemic (translocated) non-selective herbicide while it is actively growing, before planting, so the chemical reaches the rhizomes.
Avoid ploughing or harrowing through the couch grass patch, which spreads rhizome pieces; clean implements.
Use mulch and a good crop stand (correct spacing, timely planting) to shade out weeds; compare costs and labour of each method.
Judgement: a combination (rotation, hand-pulling, fertility, systemic herbicide on couch) works best because no single method removes both weeds.

parts.explanation: An integrated, multi-season programme with reasons for each method.

explanation: Identify and classify weeds, compare the costs of weed control programmes and plan long-term control.
hints: Work out each programme's cost per hectare.
Multiply by the area for whole-field figures.
For the long part, think over several seasons: witchweed seeds live for years.
